L24@P0: PMod(Sg,n) is endowed with a class of finite index subgroups called congruence subgroups. For each characteristic subgroup K of π1(Sg,n), we have an
L25@P0: induced homomorphism PMod(Sg,n) → Out(π1(Sg,n/K)). When K is finite
L26@P0: index, the kernel of the induced homomorphism is a finite index subgroup
L27@P0: of PMod(Sg,n). These subgroups are called principal congruence subgroups
L28@P0: (see Section 2 for a more general discussion) and any finite index subgroup
L29@P0: Received September 19, 2012.
L30@P0: 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. 20F36, 20E36, 20E26.
L31@P0: Key words and phrases. Congruence subgroup problem, pure braid groups.
L32@P0: Partially supported by DMS-1105710.
L33@P0: ISSN 1076-9803/2012
L34@P0-1: 925926 D. B. MCREYNOLDS
L35@P1: of PMod(Sg,n) containing a principal congruence subgroup is called a congruence subgroup. The purpose of this article is to address the following
L36@P1: problem sometimes called the congruence subgroup problem (see [2], [10]):
L37@P1: Congruence Subgroup Problem. Is every subgroup of PMod(Sg,n) of
L38@P1: finite index a congruence subgroup?
L39@P1: The congruence subgroup problem for PMod(Sg,n) is a central problem for understanding Mod(Sg,n) and PMod(Sg,n). A positive answer allows one a means of understanding the finite index subgroup structure of
L40@P1: Mod(Sg,n) and thus profinite completion of Mod(Sg,n). A few potential applications are a more precise understanding of the subgroup growth asymptotics for Mod(Sg,n) and a better understanding of the absolute Galois group
L41@P1: Gal(Q/Q) via its action on the profinite completion of Mod(Sg,n). The first
L42@P1: case to be resolved was for g = 0, n > 0 by Diaz–Donagi–Harbater [6] in
L43@P1: 1989 (though explicitly stated in the article only for n = 4). Asada [1,
L44@P1: Theorem 3A, Theorem 5] gave a proof for g = 0, 1 and n > 0 in 2001 (for
L45@P1: g = 1, see also [5] and [7]). Boggi [3, Theorem 6.1] claimed a general solution to the congruence subgroup problem in 2006. However, a gap in [3,
L46@P1: Theorem 5.4] was discovered by Abromovich, Kent, and Wieland1(see the
L47@P1: forthcoming articles [11, 12] for more on this). Boggi [4, Theorem 3.5] has
